question: A ‘rare disease’ is a disease which affects fewer than 5 in 10 000 people. It is estimated that up to 36 million people in the EU are affected by one of the 6 000 existing rare diseases. Most rare diseases are genetic, debilitating, untreatable or even fatal, and have no known cure. The immediate hope for patients often lies in clinical research into new drugs.

For example, CTI-1601 – the lead compound of the American laboratory Larimar – has been designated1 as an orphan medicinal product by the European Medicines Agency (EMA)2 for Friedreich’s ataxia (a serious neurodegenerative disease affecting an estimated 20 000 patients in Europe and 5 000 patients in the United States3) and could potentially provide a new drug therapy for this disease.

The laboratory is apparently conducting its clinical trials outside Europe. According to some patients, the laboratory is refusing to supply this product before the marketing authorisation procedure has taken place, even though its use has been authorised by the French health authorities. So far, the EMA is refusing to get involved in providing patients with access to tested or authorised treatments4.

Enrolling in clinical trials is one of the only ways to access drug therapy. How could the Commission and the EMA encourage laboratories in Europe or further afield to conduct the majority or a significant proportion of their clinical trials in Europe with patients who wish to do so?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2024) The marketing authorisation of medicinal products ensures that patients only access products that are proven to be safe and effective following the completion of clinical trials. The process for the authorisation, conduct and supervision of clinical trials remains a responsibility of Member States.

The Accelerating Clinical Trials (ACT) EU initiative1, launched by the Commission, the Heads of Medicines Agencies, and the European Medicines Agency (EMA), aims to promote clinical research in the EU. It recently established a Multi-stakeholder Platform2 with an Advisory Group including two representatives from Rare Diseases Europe (Eurordis), where stakeholders can highlight their priorities in clinical research.
ACT EU also performs monthly monitoring of clinical trials applications per therapeutic area, including statistics on rare diseases3.

Furthermore, the Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) 536/20144 requires sponsors to provide a description of the groups and subgroups of people participating in the clinical trial, including, where relevant, groups of people with specific needs, including those with rare and ultra rare diseases.

In addition, at the stage of an application for a marketing authorisation of a medicinal product, the EMA receives clinical reports in which applicants must demonstrate that their findings can be extrapolated to such populations, if that population is not sufficiently represented in the trials.
